blocks.title: Help draw out, not direct
paragraphs: Start with a question, listen for the person’s own insight, and consider a small next step. Work, home, relationships, church, and community all offer places to serve.

readings.title: Purpose conversations — six questions and how to use them
paragraphs: Helping someone explore their design does not require complicated coaching methods. Often the most meaningful progress comes through thoughtful questions and attentive listening. Leaders, mentors, and ministry teams can use the following questions to help participants reflect on how their design may connect with opportunities for service and growth.
These conversations are not intended to force quick answers. Instead, they create space for individuals to notice patterns, recognize possibilities, and begin taking faithful steps forward.
1. Where do you feel most energized when serving others?

People often discover clues about their design in the places where they feel naturally engaged and alive. These moments may reveal environments where their gifts and strengths are functioning most naturally.
2. What kinds of needs or problems consistently capture your attention?
God often places a particular awareness in our hearts toward certain needs. The issues that move us deeply may reveal areas where our design is meant to contribute.
3. Where have others recognized your contribution?

Sometimes others see patterns in our lives before we fully recognize them ourselves. Reflecting on feedback from trusted people can provide valuable insight into how our design is already serving others.
4. What opportunities around you feel like a natural place to begin serving?
Purpose often grows through small steps of faith rather than dramatic changes. Identifying simple opportunities to serve can help participants begin applying their design in practical ways.
5. What challenges or obstacles are you currently facing as you move forward?
Honest conversations about obstacles allow leaders and mentors to provide encouragement, wisdom, and support as individuals continue exploring their purpose.
6. What might the next faithful step look like for you right now?
Purpose unfolds over time. Helping someone identify the next step encourages action without creating pressure to solve everything at once.

The goal of these conversations is not to direct someone’s path but to help them listen more closely to how God may be leading them. As leaders ask thoughtful questions and provide encouragement, participants often gain clarity and confidence in the design God has placed within them.
Over time these simple conversations can become powerful moments where individuals begin recognizing the good works God prepared for them to do.

readings.title: Moving from discovery into purpose
paragraphs: The DYDD journey is designed to help participants recognize how God has shaped their life and how that design may connect with the good works He has prepared. As participants move toward the final sessions of the course, the focus begins shifting from discovery toward application.

Leaders play an important role in helping participants make this transition. Many individuals gain meaningful insight during the course but may still feel uncertain about how to apply what they have learned. Encouragement, clarity, and practical guidance can help participants begin taking the next steps of faith.
Scripture reminds us that God’s design for our lives is not simply something to understand but something to live.
“For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.”Ephesians 2:10 (NIV)

The purpose of this stage in the journey is to help participants move from reflection into faithful action. This does not mean that every participant will immediately know the full direction of their calling. Instead, the goal is to help individuals begin taking the next step of obedience as they explore how their design may serve others.
Helping Participants Discover Their Niche

The concept of niche represents the intersection where a person’s design begins to meet the needs around them. By this point in the DYDD journey, participants have explored identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts. The niche process invites them to consider how these elements may come together in meaningful ways.

Leaders should remind participants that discovering a niche is not about identifying a permanent title or position. Instead, it represents a growing awareness of how God may be inviting them to contribute within their current season of life.

Participants may begin noticing patterns such as the types of people they feel drawn toward, the problems they feel motivated to address, or the environments where their contribution seems to bring life and clarity to others.

Encourage participants to approach this process with openness and humility. Clarity often grows through experience rather than immediate certainty. What begins as a small step of service can eventually grow into a much clearer sense of direction over time.
Leader Guidance

Leaders can help participants explore their niche by asking reflective questions and encouraging them to notice patterns in their experiences. Invite participants to consider where they feel most energized when serving others, what types of needs consistently draw their attention, and where others have recognized their contribution. These conversations help participants begin connecting their design with real opportunities.
Connecting Design to Ministry Opportunities
As participants begin recognizing their niche, leaders can help them consider practical ways their design might serve others within the church and community.

Church environments often provide a wide variety of opportunities where individuals can contribute meaningfully. Some participants may feel drawn toward relational ministries such as care, mentoring, or hospitality. Others may find themselves energized by teaching, organizing, building systems, or initiating new ideas.
Encouraging participants to explore ministry opportunities that align with their design helps them move from reflection into real-life application.

Leaders can also remind participants that purpose is not limited to formal church roles. Many people live out their design through their work, family relationships, friendships, and community involvement. The good works described in Ephesians 2:10 often appear in ordinary settings where faithfulness and service are lived out day by day.
When participants begin seeing how their design connects with opportunities around them, purpose becomes more tangible and accessible.
Leader Guidance

Leaders should actively help participants identify opportunities where their design may serve others. This may include introducing them to ministry leaders, suggesting volunteer roles that align with their strengths, or encouraging them to explore ways their work and relationships outside the church can become meaningful expressions of service.
Encouraging Action and Experimentation

One of the most helpful ways participants can grow in understanding their design is through action. Trying new opportunities, serving in different roles, or exploring areas of interest often provides clarity that reflection alone cannot produce.

Leaders should encourage participants to approach this stage with a spirit of experimentation. Not every opportunity will become a long-term calling, but each experience can provide valuable insight into how a person’s design functions in real situations.

This approach removes the pressure of needing to find the perfect role immediately. Instead, participants can begin viewing opportunities as learning experiences that help them grow in awareness and confidence.
Scripture encourages believers to actively use what God has entrusted to them.
“Each of you should use whatever gift you have received to serve others, as faithful stewards of God’s grace in its various forms.”1 Peter 4:10 (NIV)
As individuals begin serving and engaging with others, their understanding of their design often becomes clearer. Action becomes a powerful teacher in the process of discovering purpose.
Leader Guidance

Encourage participants to try opportunities without feeling pressure to find the perfect role immediately. Remind them that experimentation often leads to clarity. Serving in different contexts allows individuals to discover how their design functions in real situations and helps them recognize where their contribution is most fruitful.
Using DesignPD for Ongoing Development

As participants begin serving and exploring ministry opportunities, many leaders eventually ask how individuals can continue growing in effectiveness and self-awareness. While the DYDD journey focuses on discovering how God has uniquely designed each believer, additional tools can sometimes help individuals better understand how they move ideas forward and collaborate with others.

DesignPD (Plan Decide Do) was developed as a complementary assessment within the DYDD framework to support this stage of development. DesignPD focuses on three important dynamics that influence how people function in leadership and teamwork.
PlanDecideDo

These three patterns help individuals understand how they naturally approach vision, decision making, and execution. Some people naturally begin with ideas and possibilities, while others focus more quickly on practical action. Some individuals process decisions through reflection and discernment, while others move quickly toward implementation. Understanding these tendencies can help believers become more self-aware and more effective as they work with others in ministry and leadership.

While DesignID helps participants recognize how they contribute within the Body of Christ, DesignPD helps them understand how they move ideas forward and collaborate with others to accomplish meaningful work.
Churches may choose to introduce DesignPD for purposes such as:
developing ministry leaders
strengthening team collaboration
supporting leadership development within the church
DesignPD is not required for the DYDD journey, but it can provide an additional layer of insight for churches that want to continue developing leaders and teams as they serve together.
Coaching and Mentoring After the Course

Although the DYDD course may conclude after several sessions, the journey of living out one’s design continues. Participants often benefit from ongoing encouragement and guidance as they begin applying what they have learned.

Church leaders, mentors, or ministry teams can play an important role in supporting participants beyond the course. Simple follow-up conversations, invitations to serve, or opportunities for reflection can help individuals continue growing in their understanding of purpose.

Mentoring relationships can also provide valuable perspective. Trusted leaders who understand the DYDD framework can help participants recognize patterns in their design, encourage their development, and help them navigate new opportunities.
The goal of this continued support is not to control a person’s direction but to walk alongside them as they continue exploring how God may be leading them.

When churches embrace this posture of encouragement and discipleship, the impact of the DYDD journey extends far beyond the course itself. Participants begin living with greater awareness of how God has shaped them and how their life can contribute to the flourishing of others and the work of His Kingdom.
Leader Guidance

Church leaders should remain attentive to participants who show a desire to continue developing their purpose. Simple follow up conversations, invitations to serve, and mentoring relationships can help individuals continue growing in confidence and direction. Even small moments of encouragement can help participants take meaningful steps forward.

readings.title: Continuing in purpose together
paragraphs: Creating Purpose Communities in Your Church

Completing the DYDD journey is not the end of the process. It is the beginning of living out the design God has placed within each believer. Churches that implement DYDD often discover that participants develop a strong sense of clarity about their design, gifts, and calling. However, individuals can still struggle to move forward when they attempt to pursue that calling alone.

Scripture reminds us that the Body of Christ was never intended to function in isolation. Each member contributes something unique that strengthens the whole. DYDD Alumni Groups provide a way for believers to continue walking in purpose together.

These gatherings create intentional spaces where people who have completed the DYDD journey can encourage one another, collaborate, solve problems, and support one another in pursuing the good works God prepared for them. This is not a social club. It is a purpose community.
Purpose of DYDD Alumni Groups
The goal is to help participants move from discovery to ongoing activation.
These gatherings help alumni:
Encourage one another in living out their design
Share opportunities for ministry and service
Collaborate across gifts and strengths
Solve real life challenges together
Expand the impact of the Body of Christ

When believers bring their different designs together, they often discover that the limitations they experience individually can be overcome collectively. A visionary may need an organizer. A teacher may need a builder. A servant may need someone to open doors. The alumni gathering becomes a place where the Body of Christ functions the way it was intended.
Who Should Participate
These groups are designed for individuals who have already completed the DYDD journey. Participants may include those who have:
Completed the DYDD class at your church
Worked through the DYDD book and workbook independently
Completed the DesignID assessment
Desire continued growth in living out their purpose
Because everyone shares the same foundation, the conversations can move quickly into meaningful and productive discussion.
Suggested Meeting Rhythm
Churches can host these gatherings:
Once per month
Every other month
Quarterly for larger groups
The goal is consistency without creating an overwhelming commitment. Most gatherings work well within 60 to 90 minutes.
Suggested Meeting Format
Each meeting should maintain a clear purpose and structure.
1. Welcome and Connection: Participants reconnect briefly and celebrate what God has been doing since the last gathering.
2. Purpose Stories: One or two participants share how they have been applying their design in ministry, work, or life.
3. Opportunity Exchange: Participants share ministry opportunities, needs, or initiatives where others might contribute.
4. Collaborative Problem Solving: Group members bring challenges they are facing related to calling, ministry, leadership, or service. The group offers perspective, wisdom, and support.
5. Prayer and Commission: Close the gathering by praying over one another and the work God is doing through the group.
The Power of Design-Based Fellowship
When people with different designs come together intentionally, something powerful happens.
Visionaries inspire movement.Teachers bring clarity.Servants mobilize care.Organizers create structure.
Instead of working in isolation, believers begin to function together as a unified Body.
The alumni gatherings help participants remember that their design is not just personal. It is relational and collaborative.
God designed His people to accomplish His work together.
Long Term Impact
Churches that maintain these alumni communities often see several long term outcomes.
Stronger ministry collaborationGreater volunteer engagementEmerging leaders stepping into new rolesMembers discovering new opportunities for serviceA deeper sense of unity within the Body
Rather than allowing the insights from DYDD to fade over time, the alumni groups help keep purpose alive and active within the church.
The Purpose Ecosystem

Churches often think of classes as standalone events. A course is offered, people attend for a few weeks, and then the experience ends. While these classes can be valuable, the long term impact is often limited because there is no ongoing structure to support what participants have discovered.
The DYDD journey is intended to function differently.

Rather than being a single program, DYDD can become part of a broader ecosystem within the church. Each component supports the others and helps believers move from discovery into sustained participation in the life and mission of the Body of Christ.
At the center of this ecosystem is the conviction found in Ephesians 2:10.
“For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.”
The purpose of the DYDD journey is to help believers discover how God has uniquely designed them for those good works.
The Discovery Stage

For many participants, the journey begins through the DYDD class. During this experience individuals explore the core components of their design, including their story, identity in Christ, developed expertise, personal desires, and spiritual gifts.

Tools such as the DesignID assessment and the Spiritual Gifts assessment provide additional clarity, helping participants understand how God has shaped them and how they naturally contribute to the Body of Christ.
This stage is about awareness and understanding. People begin to recognize patterns in their lives and see how God has been preparing them for meaningful contribution.
However, discovery alone is not the ultimate goal.
The Activation Stage

As participants begin applying what they have learned, many discover new opportunities to serve, lead, and contribute within the church and community. They may begin volunteering in ministries, initiating projects, mentoring others, or stepping into leadership roles.
This stage represents movement from insight into action.
Yet many believers still face challenges as they attempt to walk out their calling. They may encounter uncertainty, capacity limits, or situations where collaboration with others becomes essential.
This is where the ecosystem continues to support them.
The Community Stage
DYDD Alumni Gatherings provide an ongoing environment where participants can continue developing their purpose together.

These gatherings allow believers who share the same foundational language of design to support one another in meaningful ways. Participants can share opportunities, seek wisdom, collaborate on ministry initiatives, and pray for one another as they pursue the work God has placed before them.

Within this community, individuals begin to experience the power of the Body of Christ functioning as it was intended. One person’s strengths support another person’s limitations. Different gifts come together to form a stronger whole.
What began as an individual journey of discovery becomes a shared experience of purpose.
The Multiplication Stage
As alumni continue engaging with one another and with the life of the church, many eventually become advocates for the DYDD journey itself.
Some participants invite others to join future classes. Others help facilitate new groups or mentor participants who are just beginning their own discovery process.
In this way the ecosystem begins to multiply.
New participants enter the journey. Alumni continue developing their purpose. Ministries within the church gain new energy and alignment as people begin serving according to their design.
Over time the church becomes a place where believers are not only attending services but actively discovering and living out the good works God prepared for them.
A Living System

When implemented well, the DYDD journey becomes more than a curriculum. It becomes a living system within the church that helps people move through discovery, activation, community, and multiplication.
The class introduces believers to their design.
The assessments provide clarity and language.
The alumni gatherings create ongoing support and collaboration.
Together these elements form a pathway that helps believers grow into the purpose God has prepared for them.
As more members of the church begin living out their design, the entire Body becomes stronger, more unified, and more effective in fulfilling the mission Christ has given His church.

The goal of the DYDD journey has never been simply to complete a class or finish a book. The goal is to help believers recognize the unique way God has designed them and then step forward into the good works He has prepared for them.

When people discover their design and begin walking in it together, the Body of Christ becomes stronger. Vision finds builders. Compassion finds servants. Wisdom finds leaders. What once felt like individual potential begins to multiply as believers support and strengthen one another in their calling.

DYDD Alumni Gatherings provide a simple way for that journey to continue. They create intentional spaces where believers encourage one another, collaborate in ministry, and help each other keep moving forward in the work God has prepared.

The following appendices provide practical tools to help churches begin implementing these gatherings. The alumni gathering agenda and launch guidance below provide practical next steps. These resources are designed to help leaders cultivate communities where believers continue living on purpose and for purpose, walking together in the good works God prepared in advance for them to do.
Lead others to discover they were created on purpose and for purpose, and help them step into the work God has prepared for them.

readings.title: An alumni gathering — full agenda and prompts
paragraphs: The purpose of DYDD Alumni Gatherings is to help participants continue living out the design God has placed within them. These meetings are not intended to become casual social gatherings. They are purposeful environments where believers encourage one another, collaborate, and help each other move forward in their calling.
Most gatherings work well within 60 to 90 minutes and should maintain a simple but intentional structure.
Opening Connection (10–15 minutes)
Begin by welcoming everyone and allowing participants to reconnect. Encourage brief conversation about what God has been doing in their lives since the last gathering.
A helpful prompt may be:
Where have you seen God using your design recently?
This short connection time helps participants shift their focus from daily life into purposeful fellowship.
Purpose Stories (10–15 minutes)
Invite one or two participants to share a short story about how they have been applying their design in ministry, work, family, or community life.

These stories are powerful because they remind the group that discovering design is meant to lead to action. Hearing real experiences also encourages others who may still be exploring how their design fits into ministry.
Stories should focus on:
What they sensed God leading them to do
How their design helped them step forward
What they learned through the experience
Opportunity Exchange (10–15 minutes)
Provide space for participants to share opportunities for service, ministry needs, or initiatives where others may contribute.
Many believers discover that opportunities open up when they simply communicate what they are working on. One person’s vision may connect perfectly with another person’s gifts.
This exchange helps members of the Body begin working together rather than pursuing purpose alone.
Collaborative Problem Solving (20–30 minutes)
This portion of the meeting allows participants to bring real challenges they are facing in ministry, leadership, work, or calling.
The group listens and offers perspective, wisdom, and encouragement.
Possible discussion prompts include:
What challenge are you currently facing as you pursue what God has placed on your heart?
Where do you feel stuck or uncertain right now?
How might others in the group help strengthen or support this effort?
This portion of the gathering often becomes the most meaningful because believers begin supporting one another in practical ways.
Prayer and Commission (10 minutes)
Close the gathering by praying for one another and for the opportunities that have been discussed.
Prayer reminds the group that purpose ultimately comes from God and that their efforts depend on His guidance and power.
Encourage participants to continue connecting with one another outside the meeting as opportunities arise.

readings.title: Launching an alumni community — six practical steps
paragraphs: Churches that host the DYDD journey often find that participants want continued opportunities to grow, connect, and live out their purpose together. DYDD Alumni Gatherings provide a simple way to sustain that momentum.
The following steps can help churches launch these gatherings successfully.
Step 1- Invite the Right Participants
These gatherings are designed for individuals who have already completed the DYDD journey.
Participants may include those who have:
Completed the DYDD class at your church
Completed the DYDD book and workbook independently
Taken the DesignID assessment
Expressed a desire to continue growing in their purpose
Because participants share a common foundation, conversations quickly move into meaningful and productive territory.
Step 2 - Choose a Consistent Rhythm
The goal is to maintain connection without creating an overwhelming commitment.
Most churches find success with one of these rhythms:
Monthly gatherings
Every other month gatherings
Quarterly gatherings for larger groups
Consistency helps the community develop naturally over time.
Step 3 - Establish Clear Expectations
It is important to communicate that these gatherings are not intended to be social clubs.
Instead, they exist to help participants:
Encourage one another in their calling
Share ministry opportunities
Collaborate across gifts and strengths
Support one another through challenges
Strengthen the Body of Christ
When expectations are clear from the beginning, the gatherings remain focused and meaningful.
Step 4 - Provide Light Facilitation
These gatherings do not require heavy leadership, but someone should guide the meeting to maintain purpose and direction.
A facilitator can help by:
Opening and closing the gathering
Guiding the conversation through the agenda
Ensuring everyone has an opportunity to participate
Keeping the discussion focused and encouraging
Often the original DYDD class leader or a mature participant can serve in this role.
Step 5 - Encourage Ongoing Collaboration
One of the most valuable outcomes of these gatherings is the relationships that form between participants.
Encourage members to:
Collaborate on ministry initiatives
Support one another’s ideas and projects
Pray for one another throughout the month
Stay connected between gatherings
As people begin working together across different gifts and strengths, the Body of Christ becomes stronger and more unified.
Step 6 - Celebrate What God Is Doing
Over time, these gatherings often lead to meaningful ministry stories and new opportunities for service. Make space to celebrate how God is working through the group.
Stories of impact encourage participants and remind the church that discovering design is not simply about knowledge. It is about joining God in the work He has prepared for His people to do.

readings.title: A culture of design — serving and multiplying together
paragraphs: The DYDD journey is more than a class or a curriculum. At its heart, it is an invitation for the church to rediscover the beauty of God’s design within His people. When believers begin to understand how God has uniquely shaped them, they often move from passive participation toward active contribution.

Churches that embrace this perspective often see greater engagement, stronger leadership development, and healthier ministry teams. Instead of asking people simply to fill roles, leaders begin helping individuals serve in ways that align with how God has designed them.
Over time, this shift can help cultivate a culture where people recognize that their life has purpose within the body of Christ.

“For just as each of us has one body with many members, and these members do not all have the same function, so in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others.” Romans 12:4–5

Building this kind of culture begins with helping individuals discover their design, but it continues as leaders intentionally create environments where those designs are valued, developed, and expressed through service.
Why Design Matters for the Body of Christ
Scripture consistently describes the church as a body made up of many parts. Each believer contributes in unique ways that strengthen and support the whole community.

When individuals understand how God has shaped them, they often gain confidence in how they can serve others. Rather than comparing themselves to others or feeling uncertain about where they belong, they begin recognizing the value of their specific contribution.

This perspective also helps churches appreciate the diversity of gifts and perspectives within their community. Some individuals bring vision and initiative, while others bring wisdom, care, clarity, or stability. Each of these expressions is needed for the health of the church.

When leaders intentionally recognize and affirm these differences, the church begins to function more like the body described in Scripture, where every member plays an important role in strengthening the whole.
Aligning People with Service and Leadership
One of the most practical benefits of a design-centered approach is the ability to align people with opportunities that fit their strengths and motivations.

Many churches struggle with volunteer fatigue or frustration when individuals serve in roles that do not align well with their design. When people are placed in environments where their natural contributions are valued, they often experience greater energy, satisfaction, and long-term commitment.

Leaders can use insights from DYDD, DesignID, and Spiritual Gifts to guide these conversations. Instead of asking only what positions need to be filled, leaders can begin asking how a person’s design might contribute to the needs of the church.
This shift encourages a healthier partnership between individuals and ministry leaders. Service becomes less about obligation and more about meaningful participation in God’s work.
Developing Leaders Through Design

Understanding design also provides valuable insight for leadership development. As individuals grow in awareness of their strengths and tendencies, they often become more intentional in how they lead and serve others.

Leaders who understand their design are often better equipped to recognize the strengths of others. This awareness can lead to healthier teams, clearer communication, and stronger collaboration within ministry environments.

Churches can use the DYDD framework to support leadership development by helping emerging leaders recognize how their identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts shape their leadership approach.
Over time, this perspective helps create leaders who are not simply filling positions but stewarding the design God has placed within them.
Multiplying the DYDD Journey

One of the most meaningful outcomes of the DYDD process occurs when participants begin sharing the journey with others. Individuals who experience clarity and encouragement through the course often feel motivated to invite friends, family members, or fellow church members to explore the same discovery.

Churches can support this multiplication by offering the course regularly and encouraging previous participants to help facilitate future groups. As new facilitators are equipped, the reach of the journey naturally expands throughout the church community.

This multiplication allows the church to continue developing a shared language around design, purpose, and contribution. Over time, this language can shape how the church welcomes new members, develops leaders, and invites people into service.
Promoting the Class in Your Church
For many churches, the most effective way to introduce the DYDD journey is through personal invitation and clear communication about the purpose of the course.

Pastors and leaders may briefly introduce the class during services, small groups, or ministry gatherings. Explaining that the course helps individuals discover how God has uniquely designed them often resonates strongly with people who are searching for greater clarity about their purpose.
Promotional materials can also include simple descriptions such as:
Discover how God has shaped your lifeUnderstand your unique design and contributionExplore how your story, gifts, and experiences connect with purpose

Personal invitations from previous participants are often the most powerful form of promotion. When individuals share how the journey helped them gain clarity or encouragement, others are naturally drawn to explore the experience themselves.
Over time, the DYDD journey can become a meaningful part of how the church helps believers grow in awareness of their design and confidence in their purpose.

readings.title: From preparation to ongoing multiplication — a church timeline
paragraphs: Church leaders often find it helpful to approach the DYDD journey with a simple plan for introducing the process within their church. While every ministry context is different, the following timeline provides a practical example of how a church might launch and sustain the DYDD journey over several months.
This approach allows leaders to introduce the framework gradually while building momentum and participation within the congregation.
Month One — Preparation

Begin by preparing the leaders who will guide the DYDD journey. This includes becoming familiar with the DYDD framework, reviewing the course materials, and identifying individuals who may help facilitate discussions or support the class.

Leaders should also begin sharing the vision for the journey within the church. This may include mentioning the upcoming class during announcements, small groups, or ministry meetings. The goal during this stage is to build awareness and invite participation.
Months Two and Three — Launch the DYDD Class
Begin the DYDD class using the eight session structure provided in the Playbook. Encourage participants to engage with the book, workbook reflections, and assessments as part of the journey.

During these weeks leaders guide participants through the discovery process, helping them explore the key components of their design including identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts. Table discussions and reflection exercises play an important role in helping participants recognize patterns in how God has shaped their lives.

As the class progresses toward the later sessions, participants begin connecting these insights through the niche process. By the end of the course many individuals will begin seeing clearer connections between their design and opportunities to serve others.
Month Four — Encourage Action

After the class concludes, leaders should help participants begin applying what they have discovered. This may include inviting them to explore ministry opportunities, encouraging conversations with ministry leaders, or supporting small experiments where participants try serving in new ways.

Purpose often becomes clearer through action. When participants begin stepping into opportunities that align with their design, they gain greater confidence and clarity about how God may be leading them.
Month Five — Launch Alumni Gatherings

As participants begin living out their design, churches can introduce DYDD Alumni Gatherings. These gatherings provide an environment where individuals can continue encouraging one another, sharing opportunities, and collaborating in ministry.
Alumni gatherings help sustain the momentum of the DYDD journey by creating a community focused on purpose, growth, and service within the Body of Christ.
Ongoing — Multiply the Journey

As the culture of design grows within the church, new participants will naturally become interested in the DYDD journey. Churches may offer the class multiple times throughout the year and invite alumni to help facilitate future sessions.
Over time this process helps create a culture where believers are continually discovering their design and stepping into the good works God has prepared for them.

readings.title: On Purpose, For Purpose
paragraphs: Session 1 — On Purpose, For Purpose

This opening session sets the foundation for the entire DYDD journey. Before participants explore the different aspects of their design, it is important that they understand the central truth guiding the process. God creates people intentionally and invites them to live with purpose within His Kingdom.

The session introduces the core theme of the journey: On Purpose, For Purpose. Participants are reminded that their life is not accidental and that God has been shaping them long before they began considering questions of calling or contribution. This conversation is rooted in Ephesians 2:8–10, which explains that believers are saved by grace, formed by God as His handiwork, and invited to walk in the good works He prepared in advance.
“For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.”Ephesians 2:10 (NIV)

This first gathering helps participants understand that discovering their design is not about striving to earn significance. Instead, it is about recognizing how God has already been shaping their life and learning to walk faithfully in what He has prepared.
Key Concepts for Leaders

Participants need to hear clearly that purpose grows out of grace. The DYDD journey does not ask people to manufacture purpose or prove their value. It invites them to recognize the work God is already doing in their life.

It is also helpful to emphasize that purpose unfolds over time. Many people enter the journey hoping for a single clear answer about their calling. Leaders can gently remind participants that clarity often develops gradually as they reflect, serve, and continue walking with God.
Relevant scripture passages can help reinforce this understanding.
Jeremiah 29:11 reminds believers that God has intentions for their future.
“For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the Lord, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.”Jeremiah 29:11 (NIV)
Psalm 139 affirms the intentional way God forms each life.
“For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother’s womb.”Psalm 139:13 (NIV)
Areas Leaders Should Watch For

Some participants may struggle with feelings that their life has lacked purpose. Others may carry disappointment from past experiences that seemed to contradict their expectations of how God would lead them. Leaders should create a welcoming environment where people can acknowledge these feelings without pressure to resolve them immediately.

Another common challenge is comparison. Participants may begin measuring their design against the gifts or experiences of others in the group. Leaders should regularly remind the group that the goal of the journey is not to rank or compare designs but to recognize the unique ways God works through each person.
Encouraging participants to listen carefully to one another and celebrate the diversity within the group helps create a healthy environment for discovery.
Discussion Focus
The primary goal of this session is to help participants begin asking a simple but important question.
What if God has been shaping my life on purpose?

Allow time for participants to reflect on where they may already see signs of God’s intentional work in their life. These early conversations begin preparing the group for the deeper exploration that will unfold throughout the rest of the journey.
Session 2 — Identity and the DesignID Assessment

This session focuses on the foundation of identity. Before participants explore how they serve or where they contribute, it is essential that they understand who they are in Christ. Identity shapes how people see themselves, how they relate to others, and how they interpret their role within the body of Christ.

The conversation begins with the biblical truth that identity is not formed by performance, achievement, or comparison. Identity is established through relationship with Christ. When believers understand whose they are, they are able to approach questions of purpose and contribution with humility, freedom, and confidence.

readings.title: Teaching outline
paragraphs: Weekly Teaching Outline — This outline provides leaders with a simple structure for guiding each session of the DYDD journey. The goal is not to deliver lengthy lectures but to introduce key ideas that help participants reflect on how God has shaped their life.
Each session should include four basic elements:

Teaching — Introduce the core idea for the sessionReflection — Participants engage with workbook exercisesDiscussion — Table conversations help participants process insightsApplication — Participants begin recognizing how the concept connects to their design
Most sessions can be completed in 75–90 minutes.
Session 1 — On Purpose, For Purpose
ObjectiveIntroduce the biblical foundation of the DYDD journey and the meaning of Ephesians 2:10.
Key Teaching Themes

God intentionally created each person with purpose.Salvation is by grace, but believers are also designed for good works.Purpose is not something we invent but something we discover as we walk with God.
Key Scripture
Ephesians 2:8–10 (NIV)
Discussion Prompts
What stood out to you about the phrase “created in Christ Jesus to do good works”?How have you thought about purpose in the past?What do you hope to discover during this journey?
Workbook Focus
Introduction to the DESIGN framework.
Session 2 — Identity and DesignID
Objective
Help participants explore their identity in Christ and introduce the DesignID assessment.
Key Teaching Themes
Identity begins with whose we are before who we are.God has uniquely designed each person to contribute in different ways.The DesignID assessment helps reveal patterns in how our design operates.

prepare.title: The outcome you are working toward
paragraphs: People leave knowing that their worth does not depend on discovering an impressive calling. They understand the journey’s purpose, feel free to participate at their own level, and know what comes next.
Anchor Scripture: Ephesians 2:8–10. Optional supporting reading: Psalm 139:13. Keep grace, intentional design, and faithful response together.

prepare.title: What to make clear
paragraphs: We are saved by grace, not achievement. We are God’s handiwork, not an accident. We are invited to walk in good works, not manufacture significance.
Purpose unfolds over time. This first gathering gives people a hopeful way to notice God’s work, not a deadline for having their future settled.

prepare.title: What to prepare
paragraphs: Review the introduction and On Purpose material assigned to this gathering. Have the digital workbook available; the book can deepen understanding but is not a replacement for reflection.
Select two or three questions rather than trying to use every prompt. Check the meeting length and location. Explain private versus chosen sharing before discussion begins.

prepare.title: What to watch for
paragraphs: Notice disappointment about past seasons, pressure to find a final answer, and comparison with someone else’s story or gifts. Respond with listening and encouragement, not a diagnosis of someone’s calling.
Your role is to make room for discovery. Use the situation-based help in Leading now when you need a practical response.

followThrough.title: Before people leave
paragraphs: Confirm the next date and assigned Identity content from the Schedule tab. Explain when to complete DesignID so participants have space to read and reflect before discussing it. Do not collect or display private results without their choice to share.

followThrough.title: Between gatherings
paragraphs: Encourage participants to return to the workbook, notice one ordinary example of God’s work, and pray about what is emerging. A private discussion reminder in their Field Kit is theirs to bring, not something sent to you.

followThrough.title: Your own brief debrief
paragraphs: What helped people feel welcome? Which questions opened conversation? Who might appreciate personal encouragement? Carry these observations into your next preparation without creating a record of someone else’s private story.

anchor.title: Belonging in Christ → understanding design → serving together
paragraphs: Galatians 3:26 · 2 Corinthians 5:17 · 1 Corinthians 12:27. Identity is received in Christ; a report helps describe contribution, not establish worth.

prepare.title: The outcome you are working toward
paragraphs: Participants leave with a clearer distinction between their secure identity in Christ and the tendencies described by DesignID. They can name one insight about contribution without treating a reflection as a fixed label.
Anchor Scripture: Galatians 3:26. Read 2 Corinthians 5:17 and 1 Corinthians 12:27 alongside it: new life and belonging come before comparison, and every part of the body matters.

prepare.title: What to make clear
paragraphs: Begin with whose we are before who we are. Identity does not come from performance, a ministry position, or an assessment result. DesignID offers language for patterns of contribution; it does not measure spiritual maturity or decide someone’s calling.

The four reflections are Architect, Artisan, Shepherd, and Steward. Introduce their different contributions with equal value. A primary reflection is a starting point for noticing patterns, not a box that excludes the others.

prepare.title: What to prepare
paragraphs: Review the Identity lessons assigned in your Circle schedule and the full readings alongside this guide. Read the DesignID assessment and interpretation guidance before explaining results. Select two or three discussion questions and adapt the example gathering flow to your meeting length.

Ask participants to review their own reports in advance if available, using the access provided in their Journey. Do not require a new purchase, promise an unprovided QR code, or assume you can see completion or private results. Participants without reports can still join the entire Identity conversation.

prepare.title: How to introduce the report
paragraphs: Start with reflections and one lived example. Then introduce integrative reflections, capacity, approaches to learning, contribution to the body, and shadow reflections only as useful. The full Identity reading explains these elements; there is no need to interpret every report section tonight.

Present any scores as whole-number points, never percentages or measures of ability. The assessment distributes five points in each of twenty statement groups; the profile describes relative patterns within one person, not a ranking between people.

prepare.title: What to watch for
paragraphs: Watch for comparison, disappointment, over-identification with a label, or discomfort sharing a report. Keep the tone curious and voluntary. Do not assign a reflection or a ministry role to another person.

Prepare one ordinary example of different contributions working together. Use Leading now for help with unexpected results, missing reports, score comparison, or a discussion that becomes too technical.

readings.title: Identity and DesignID — full session guidance
paragraphs: “So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith.”Galatians 3:26 (NIV)

This session also introduces the DesignID assessment. DesignID is a tool that helps participants recognize how their identity and contribution tend to express themselves within community and ministry. Rather than measuring personality traits or preferences alone, the assessment highlights patterns of reflection and contribution that often shape how a person engages with others and participates in the work of the church.

The DesignID results identify one of four primary reflections that represent different ways people naturally contribute. These reflections help participants recognize the lens through which they often see problems, opportunities, and relationships. Understanding this reflection gives participants language for how their design may show up in leadership, service, teamwork, and ministry environments.

Participants are encouraged to complete the DesignID assessment during this stage of the journey. The insights gained from the report will serve as a helpful framework as they continue exploring expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts in the sessions that follow.
Key Concepts for Leaders

Identity must remain rooted in Christ, not in an assessment result. DesignID is a helpful tool for reflection and insight, but it should never replace the deeper truth of who a person is as a child of God.

Leaders should emphasize that the assessment provides language for understanding tendencies, not labels that limit a person. The goal is to help participants notice patterns in how God has shaped them so they can better understand their contribution within the body of Christ.
Another important concept is the diversity of design within the church. Scripture teaches that the body of Christ is made up of many different parts, each contributing in unique ways.
“Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.”1 Corinthians 12:27 (NIV)
When participants begin to see how their reflection differs from others in the group, it often creates appreciation for the variety of ways God works through His people.
Areas Leaders Should Watch For

Some participants may place too much importance on the assessment result. Leaders should remind the group that DesignID is simply a tool that helps bring language to what may already be present in their life and experiences.

Others may struggle if their result feels unexpected or unclear. Encourage participants to read the report thoughtfully and discuss their insights with others in the group. Often, community conversation helps confirm and clarify what the assessment reveals.

Leaders should also watch for comparison. Participants may be tempted to view certain reflections as more valuable or more spiritual than others. Scripture reminds us that every role within the body of Christ is important and necessary.
Discussion Focus
This session invites participants to consider two important questions.
What does it mean for my identity to be rooted in Christ?
How might the way God designed me influence how I contribute to the body of Christ?
These conversations help participants begin recognizing how their identity and reflection provide a foundation for the rest of the DYDD journey.
DesignID Overview

DesignID is introduced during the Identity portion of the DYDD journey because it helps participants understand how their identity often expresses itself in community, leadership, and service. While identity in Christ forms the spiritual foundation of who we are, DesignID provides helpful language for recognizing how our design tends to show up in real life.

The assessment helps participants identify patterns in how they perceive situations, process information, relate to others, and contribute to the work of the church. Rather than defining a person or limiting their potential, DesignID offers insight into natural tendencies that often shape how individuals engage with people, opportunities, and challenges.

As participants move through the remaining sections of the DYDD journey, the DesignID insights serve as a helpful lens for understanding how their expertise, story, desires, and spiritual gifts may combine to influence their contribution.

The goal of introducing DesignID at this stage is not to analyze every detail of the report. Instead, it simply helps participants begin recognizing how God may have uniquely shaped their perspective and contribution within the body of Christ.
DesignID Elements Overview:
Element
What it is
Why it matters
Reflections
Reflections identify the primary way a person tends to see the world and respond to opportunities, challenges, and relationships.
Understanding a reflection helps participants recognize how they naturally contribute within teams, ministries, and leadership environments.
Integrative Reflections
Integrative reflections describe how two reflections often work together to shape a person’s broader perspective and approach to collaboration.
These integrations help participants see how their design may bridge different perspectives within the body of Christ.
Capacity
Capacity describes the current level of energy and strength a person has available within each reflection.
Recognizing capacity helps participants understand where they may currently operate with strength, balance, or limitation and encourages healthy stewardship of their energy.
Approaches to Learning
This area describes how individuals often prefer to learn, process information, and grow in understanding.
Understanding learning tendencies helps participants develop in ways that align with how they naturally absorb and apply new insight.
Contribution to the Body
This portion of the report highlights how a person’s reflection often expresses itself within the body of Christ.

readings.title: Understanding DesignID and its assessment format
paragraphs: The DesignID Assessment

The DesignID assessment is an important part of the DYDD journey. While the class itself focuses on reflection, discussion, and discovery, DesignID provides participants with structured insight into how their design often expresses itself in real life. The assessment helps individuals recognize patterns in how they perceive situations, approach challenges, and contribute within community and ministry.

Within the DYDD process, DesignID supports the Identity portion of the journey. It provides language and perspective that help participants better understand the lens through which they often see the world and how that perspective may influence their leadership, relationships, and service. As participants continue through Expertise, Story, Desire, and Spiritual Gifts, the DesignID insights often help clarify how these different elements interact within their design.

Leaders may also find that the assessment has application beyond the DYDD class. Churches and organizations often use DesignID to strengthen team alignment, develop leaders, improve communication within ministry teams, and help individuals understand how their contribution complements others in the body of Christ. These broader applications reinforce the value of the assessment as a tool for ongoing development and service.
Access and preparation for your Circle

Use the DesignID access and assessment instructions provided in each participant’s current Journey account. Check the actual Circle schedule for when results will be discussed. A separate purchase or group code is not a new requirement created by this guide. If access or report delivery needs help, resolve that individually without holding up the group or collecting private results.
Assessment Development and Credibility

DesignID was developed to provide meaningful insight while maintaining strong measurement discipline. The assessment measures how a person’s design energy tends to distribute across four core reflections: Architect, Artisan, Shepherd, and Steward. These reflections represent different ways individuals often contribute within relationships, teams, and ministry environments.

Participants respond to a series of statement groups that require thoughtful choices rather than simple agreement or disagreement. The design intentionally captures tradeoffs in how individuals naturally allocate their energy and attention across different types of contributions.
The instrument uses an ipsative fixed sum response format. Participants complete twenty groups of four statements and must allocate exactly five points across the four options in each group.

This design offers several advantages for accuracy. Because participants must distribute points across all four options, they cannot simply agree strongly with every statement. The forced allocation encourages careful consideration and reveals relative preference and energy distribution more clearly than traditional rating scales.

Across the full assessment, participants distribute a total of one hundred points across the four reflections. This produces a compositional profile that shows how design energy is distributed within the individual.

This approach helps reveal patterns of contribution rather than measuring ability or value. The goal of the assessment is to illuminate how a person’s design tends to express itself, not to rank individuals or determine spiritual maturity.

Leaders should remind participants that the assessment is one tool within the larger DYDD journey. It provides helpful language and insight, but it works best when considered alongside the workbook reflections, group discussions, spiritual gifts assessment, and prayerful discernment over time.
When used in this way, DesignID becomes a powerful aid in helping participants recognize how God has uniquely shaped them to love, live, and lead within the good works He has prepared.

readings.title: Interpreting DesignID together
paragraphs: Interpreting DesignID Results in Group Settings

For many leaders, reviewing DesignID results with a group can feel like one of the more challenging parts of facilitating the DYDD journey. Participants often arrive at this point with curiosity about what their results mean and how they relate to the rest of their design. With the right approach and the supporting materials provided, this portion of the process can become one of the most engaging and meaningful moments in the entire experience.

It is important for leaders to remember that the goal of this session is not to analyze every detail of each participant’s report. Instead, the objective is to help individuals begin recognizing patterns in their results and understanding how their reflection and capacity may influence the way they contribute within relationships, teams, and ministry.
Use the teaching guidance below with participants’ own reports. Teaching-slide PDFs and additional handouts are not attached to this session yet; this reading provides the concepts you can use now.

Begin with the rationale behind DesignID and how the assessment supports the broader DYDD journey. Remind participants that the assessment helps reveal how design energy may naturally distribute across different forms of contribution.
Introduce the four reflections that appear within the report. These describe four primary ways individuals often express their design.
Architect often expresses through creation and movement.
Artisan often expresses through clarity and insight.
Shepherd often expresses through connection and care.
Steward often expresses through continuity and stability.

Explain the concept of capacity using participants’ reports. Help participants understand how their design energy may function in different levels of availability or strain: energized, steady, stretched, or depleted.
Introduce shadow reflections. Every strength carries potential challenges if it becomes overextended or disconnected from healthy balance. Encourage humility and awareness rather than criticism.
Invite participants to explore the motivations, contributions, and tendencies associated with each reflection in their own reports.
Leaders are encouraged to present this material slowly and allow time for participants to consider how the descriptions connect with their own experience.
Supporting Resources for Group Interpretation
For deeper engagement, begin with the participant’s own report and the guidance in this session.

Group patterns can be discussed through examples people choose to share. No score-collection spreadsheet is supplied here, and Circle membership does not give leaders access to private results. Do not require scores, rank participants, or use group averages to evaluate someone’s worth or spiritual maturity.
Additional handouts may support deeper exploration when supplied. They are not required to use this guide.
The report’s capacity, learning, and contribution sections can support reflection on different energy states and patterns of service. A separate Full Capacity Matrix handout is not attached here.
These materials allow leaders to expand the conversation if the group shows interest while still keeping the primary focus on personal discovery and reflection.
Guidance for Leaders

When facilitating this session, leaders should emphasize curiosity rather than certainty. Participants are not expected to fully understand every aspect of their report immediately. Instead, they are invited to begin noticing patterns that resonate with their experiences and observations.

It is also helpful to remind participants that the assessment describes tendencies rather than limitations. The goal is not to place people into categories but to help them recognize how their design may naturally express itself.

Leaders should also encourage participants to hold their results with humility and openness. As individuals continue serving, learning, and growing within community, their understanding of their design often becomes clearer and more refined over time.

When approached in this spirit of discovery, interpreting DesignID results becomes less about technical explanation and more about helping participants recognize how God may be uniquely shaping their contribution within the body of Christ.

readings.title: Facilitation — full guidance
paragraphs: The Role of the Facilitator

The facilitator plays an important role in guiding participants through the DYDD journey. This role is less about teaching expertise and more about creating an environment where people can reflect, share, and discover how God has been shaping their life.

A facilitator helps guide the rhythm of each session by introducing the main ideas, encouraging conversation, and allowing space for participants to process what they are learning. Rather than providing all the answers, the facilitator helps participants ask thoughtful questions and notice the ways God may already be at work in their life.

The goal of the facilitator is to create a setting where individuals feel seen, heard, and valued. As participants share their reflections, the facilitator helps maintain a respectful and encouraging atmosphere where people can speak openly and listen well to one another.
Scripture reminds leaders that growth within the church happens as people are equipped and encouraged to serve.

“So Christ himself gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the pastors and teachers, to equip his people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up.”Ephesians 4:11–12 (NIV)

In this sense, the facilitator serves as a guide who helps participants move through the journey of discovery. By encouraging reflection, conversation, and prayer, facilitators help individuals begin recognizing how God has designed them and where He may be inviting them to serve.
Key Concepts for Facilitators
Facilitators guide the process rather than control it. The DYDD journey works best when participants are given time to think, reflect, and speak for themselves.

Listening is one of the most important leadership skills in this role. Participants often gain clarity as they share their insights with others, so creating space for thoughtful conversation is essential.

Facilitators should encourage curiosity and reflection rather than trying to interpret someone’s design for them. The goal is to help participants discover how God has been shaping their life, not to assign conclusions.
Facilitators should also model humility and openness. When leaders approach the journey with curiosity and faith, it helps participants feel comfortable doing the same.
Areas Facilitators Should Watch For

Facilitators should be mindful of participants who may dominate conversation as well as those who may hesitate to speak. Encouraging balanced participation helps ensure everyone has the opportunity to share.

It is also important to watch for moments when discussions drift toward giving advice rather than listening. The purpose of the conversations is to explore and reflect, not to correct or direct someone else’s journey.

Facilitators should gently redirect conversations that move into comparison or judgment. Each participant’s design and story are unique, and the goal is to celebrate that diversity rather than measure one person against another.
Encouraging a posture of respect, curiosity, and prayer throughout the journey helps create the environment where participants can engage deeply and grow together.
Creating a Culture of Discovery

One of the most important responsibilities of a leader during the DYDD journey is helping cultivate an environment where discovery can take place. Participants will be reflecting on personal experiences, spiritual questions, and areas of growth, so the overall culture of the group should be welcoming, supportive, and respectful.

A healthy culture of discovery begins with hospitality. Participants should feel that they are entering a space where they are valued and where their voice matters. Simple practices such as greeting people warmly, learning names, and encouraging conversation help create an atmosphere where individuals feel comfortable engaging with the material and with one another.

Trust is also essential. Many of the conversations throughout the DYDD journey invite participants to reflect on personal experiences and spiritual growth. When people feel safe to share honestly without fear of judgment or comparison, they are much more likely to engage deeply in the process. Leaders can support this environment by modeling humility, listening carefully, and responding with encouragement.

Another important element of a discovery culture is curiosity. Participants should be reminded that the goal of the journey is not to arrive at perfect answers but to explore how God has been shaping their life. Questions, reflection, and thoughtful discussion are part of the process. When curiosity is welcomed, participants often begin noticing connections in their story and design that they had not previously considered.

A nurturing environment also encourages mutual support within the group. As participants listen to one another’s experiences and insights, they begin to recognize the many ways God is working through different individuals. This shared discovery strengthens relationships and helps participants appreciate the diversity of gifts and perspectives within the body of Christ.
Scripture reminds us that growth in faith often happens within community.
“Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.”1 Thessalonians 5:11 (NIV)

When a culture of encouragement and discovery is present, participants are more likely to engage honestly, support one another, and remain open to the ways God may be shaping their understanding throughout the journey.
Leading Effective Table Discussions

Table discussions are one of the most important parts of the DYDD journey. While teaching introduces the concepts, conversation is often where participants begin recognizing how those ideas connect to their own life. As individuals listen to one another, share reflections, and ask questions, they often discover insights that might not emerge through reading or teaching alone.

Leaders should view table discussions as an essential part of the learning process rather than simply an optional activity. These conversations allow participants to process what they are learning in community, which often leads to deeper understanding and stronger relationships within the group.

Effective table discussions begin with clear and simple questions. Prompts should invite reflection rather than demand perfect answers. Questions that begin with phrases such as “What stood out to you,” “Where have you seen this in your life,” or “What are you beginning to notice” help participants engage naturally with the conversation.

Facilitators should also encourage balanced participation. Some individuals are comfortable speaking quickly, while others need time to think before sharing. A healthy discussion environment allows space for both. Leaders can gently invite quieter participants to share while also guiding the conversation so that no one voice dominates the group.

Listening is one of the most valuable skills during table discussions. Participants should be encouraged to listen carefully to one another without immediately offering advice or correction. Often the most helpful response is simply acknowledging what someone has shared and allowing the group to reflect together.
Scripture reminds us that wisdom often grows through listening and thoughtful conversation.
“My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry.”James 1:19 (NIV)

Leaders should also help keep conversations aligned with the purpose of the session. Discussions may occasionally drift into unrelated topics or personal debates. When this happens, facilitators can gently guide the group back to the reflection questions and the purpose of the session.

Table discussions are not meant to produce perfect conclusions. Their purpose is to help participants reflect on their experiences, recognize patterns in their design, and learn from the insights of others. When conversations remain respectful, curious, and encouraging, these moments often become some of the most meaningful parts of the entire journey.
Helping Participants Process Their Design

As participants move through the DYDD journey, they will begin noticing patterns in their identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts. Processing these insights thoughtfully is an important part of the experience. Leaders play a helpful role by guiding participants as they reflect on what they are learning and how the different pieces of their design begin to connect.

Participants often need time to recognize how the various elements of their life fit together. Rather than rushing toward conclusions, leaders should encourage a posture of reflection, prayer, and curiosity. The goal is not to force a quick answer about purpose but to help individuals notice the ways God may already be shaping their life and inviting them forward.

The workbook plays an important role in this process. The C.A.R.E. reflections help participants slow down and engage with what they are learning. By connecting, acting, reflecting, and exploring, individuals begin to see how their experiences, abilities, and spiritual gifts interact with one another. Leaders should regularly encourage participants to revisit their workbook reflections as they process their design.

It is also helpful for participants to discuss their insights with others in the group. Hearing how others perceive their strengths or contributions can often provide confirmation or clarity that individuals may not see on their own. These conversations reinforce the biblical picture of the church as a community where believers help one another grow.
Scripture reminds us that wisdom and understanding often develop through counsel and shared insight.
“Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.”Proverbs 15:22 (NIV)

Leaders should remind participants that discovering their design is not about creating a perfect description of who they are. Instead, it is about recognizing how God has been shaping their life and beginning to walk faithfully in the direction He is leading.

Processing design also requires humility and openness. Some participants may initially struggle to recognize their strengths, while others may discover aspects of their design they had not previously considered. Encouraging participants to hold their insights with both gratitude and curiosity helps keep the journey focused on growth rather than certainty.

Ultimately, the role of the leader is to help participants see connections. As identity, expertise, story, desire, and spiritual gifts begin to align, individuals often gain a clearer picture of how their life may contribute to the body of Christ and to the good works God has prepared for them.
Common Questions and How to Respond

As participants move through the DYDD journey, it is natural for questions to arise. Many individuals are exploring aspects of their life and faith in ways they may not have considered before. Leaders should welcome these questions and approach them with patience, humility, and encouragement.

The role of the leader is not to provide every answer but to help guide participants toward thoughtful reflection, prayer, and conversation. Many questions are best explored within community rather than solved immediately.
Several types of questions commonly arise during the journey.

Some participants may ask whether they have identified their purpose correctly. It is helpful to remind them that the goal of the journey is not to produce a final answer but to begin recognizing patterns in how God has shaped their life. Purpose often becomes clearer as individuals continue walking in obedience.
Scripture reminds us that God guides His people step by step.
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.”Proverbs 3:5–6 (NIV)

Others may wonder if their design seems too ordinary or unimportant. Leaders can encourage participants by reminding them that God works through everyday faithfulness. Many of the most meaningful contributions within the church happen through simple acts of service, encouragement, and leadership.
“Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much.”Luke 16:10 (NIV)

Some participants may feel uncertain about their assessment results or struggle to see how the different parts of their design fit together. Leaders should encourage them to view the assessments and reflections as tools for discovery rather than final conclusions. Insight often grows over time through prayer, experience, and the affirmation of others in community.

There may also be participants who compare their design with others in the group. Leaders should gently remind the group that diversity is an intentional part of God’s design for the church. Each person contributes in a different way, and every role is valuable.
“Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.”1 Corinthians 12:27 (NIV)

Finally, some individuals may feel hesitant about taking a next step. They may worry about making the wrong decision or moving in the wrong direction. Leaders can reassure participants that God often leads through small steps of faithfulness rather than immediate clarity about the entire path.
Encouraging participants to remain prayerful, attentive, and open to God’s guidance helps them approach the journey with confidence and humility.

The purpose of responding to questions is not to resolve every uncertainty but to help participants remain engaged in the process of discovery. As they continue reflecting, serving, and walking with God, clarity about their design and contribution will often grow naturally over time.
